definition: A fixed-size vector capturing voice identity, trained on speaker-discrimination tasks.
details: A fixed-size vector capturing voice identity, trained on speaker-discrimination tasks. Used for speaker verification, diarization, and as the conditioning signal in multi-speaker and cloned TTS.

explainer.lead: A d-vector turns speech into a fixed-size numerical description of who is speaking. That shared voice-identity representation lets systems check whether two voices match, separate speakers in a conversation, or give a text-to-speech system a particular voice.

tiers.eli5: A d-vector is like a short numerical description of a voice. A computer learns to make these descriptions by practising telling different speakers apart. It can then compare voices or use one description to make synthetic speech sound like a chosen speaker.
tiers.practitioner: Use d-vectors as speaker representations for verification, diarization, or conditioning multi-speaker and cloned TTS. Their fixed size makes them convenient to pass between these stages. A match is evidence about speaker identity, not proof, and a vector intended for verification should not automatically be assumed suitable for high-quality voice cloning.
tiers.paperLevel: For speech input x, a model f_theta trained with a speaker-discrimination objective produces d = f_theta(x), where d is in R^D and D is fixed. The vector represents speaker identity and can be compared with other speaker vectors or supplied as conditioning to multi-speaker or cloned TTS. Speaker discrimination during training does not by itself guarantee reliable identification in every downstream setting.

explainer.example: For speaker verification, create d-vectors from a person's enrollment speech and from a new recording. The system compares the vectors to decide whether the new voice matches the enrolled speaker; the same kind of vector could instead condition a TTS system on that speaker's voice.

usedIn.name: Speaker verification
usedIn.detail: Represent speech so a system can assess whether voices belong to the same speaker.

usedIn.name: Speaker diarization
usedIn.detail: Provide voice-identity features that help distinguish speakers in a recording.

usedIn.name: Multi-speaker text-to-speech
usedIn.detail: Condition speech generation on a vector representing the desired speaker.

usedIn.name: Voice-cloning text-to-speech
usedIn.detail: Supply the speaker-identity signal used to synthesize speech in a target voice.

explainer.intuition: Instead of storing a whole recording to describe a voice, compress the speaker-related information into one list of numbers. Training the model to discriminate between speakers encourages that list to capture voice identity.
howItWorks: Provide speech as input to the d-vector model.
Train the model on tasks that require distinguishing speakers.
Produce a vector with the same fixed size for each input.
Use the vector to compare speakers or to condition speech synthesis.
explainer.whyItMatters: One fixed-size representation connects several speaker-aware tasks, avoiding a different voice description for each application. It is especially useful when speech synthesis must be controlled by speaker identity.
misconceptions: A d-vector is not a recording or a reconstruction of the spoken words.
A fixed-size vector does not mean every speaker can be identified perfectly.
A d-vector is not automatically suitable for every verification, diarization, and cloning system.
